activities.anchor: Nobody can write the rule for what spam looks like
activities.caption: bet first — why rules refuse to work
activities.name: hmlSpamPredict

config.q: For most of computing's history, programs were rules written by humans. Why does spam refuse to be written as rules?
choices: email is encrypted, so no rule can read it
spam is 'whatever spammers decide this month' — they change tactics the moment a list works
spam is too rare to be worth writing rules about
config.why: The signs — odd senders, urgency, misspellings — work once, then the spammers change tactics. The fix was not better rules but a different way of building software: a learning loop.

activities.anchor: Instead of writing rules, you write a
activities.caption: rebuild the loop — guess, measure, step
activities.name: hmlLoopOrder

config.prompt: The loop that trains everything from spam filters to ChatGPT-class models — put it in order:
items: a loss function measures how wrong the guess was
calculus supplies the direction of downhill — the gradient
each adjustable parameter takes a small step that way
repeat a few million times — behaviour no one programmed emerges
config.why: Machines 'learn' by systematically reducing a mistake score against data — not by acquiring understanding.

activities.anchor: Supervised tasks split into two families
activities.caption: file the examples — three ways to learn
activities.name: hmlParadigmBuckets

config.prompt: Three paradigms, one map — file each example:

items.label: which customers cluster together, which words appear together
an agent acts, receives rewards, learns which actions pay off
how systems learned to play Go and control robots

config.why: Supervised learning infers mappings from labelled examples; unsupervised finds structure without labels; reinforcement learns from a score that arrives late.

activities.anchor: The prototype of supervised learning is the
activities.caption: pair each tree term with its meaning
activities.name: hmlTreeMatch

config.prompt: The decision tree, read properly — pair the parts:

pairs.right: chooses each split by information gain
the question that most reduces uncertainty goes first
but grown from examples instead of played for fun

config.why: Trees are beloved for one reason: you can read them — which is also what makes them easy to overfit.

activities.anchor: the machine does not "figure out the rules"
activities.caption: find the faulty line — what the machine actually does
activities.name: hmlRulesSpot

config.prompt: This explanation contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The machine adjusts numbers to reduce a score.
A spam filter has no concept of deception; it has weights that happened to distinguish the labelled examples.
When the world shifts — new spam tactics, a hospital changing scanners — the model notices on its own and adapts without retraining.
The shift has a name: concept drift.
Spam is 'whatever spammers decide this month'.
config.correction: The model does not notice the shift — it must be retrained; drifting worlds are exactly where memorised weights fail.
config.why: The machine never 'figured out the rules' in any human sense — it adjusted numbers against a score, so a changed world is invisible to it until the data says so.

activities.anchor: The defence is procedural and simple
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the split that keeps you honest
activities.name: hmlSplitCloze

config.text: Train on one portion. Evaluate on a %%0%% the model never saw, and tune on that. Report final performance on a third %%1%%, touched exactly once. When data is scarce, %%2%% rotates the split k times and averages.
config.hint: One set to tune on, one touched exactly once, and a rotation trick for scarce data.

activities.anchor: penalising model complexity inside the loss itself
activities.caption: drag the divider — memoriser versus generaliser
activities.name: hmlRazorCompare

config.prompt: Overfitting in two portraits — drag between them:

before.label: The memoriser
before.text: Leaves like 'sender contains the letter q' — rules that fit the sample; a student who memorises last year's answers word for word, then fails the new exam.

after.label: The generaliser
after.text: Simpler explanations that fit the data extend to new data — Ockham's razor wearing a loss function: regularisation, pruning, the widened train-validation gap as the alarm.

config.why: You train on the data you have but are graded on data you do not have — the only score that matters is on unseen data.

activities.anchor: Each step multiplies the error by
activities.caption: which curve is the loss decay?
activities.name: hmlDecayTrace

config.prompt: The hand-computed loop: η = 0.5 of the error removed per step. Which curve shows the loss after n training steps?
config.why: 10 → 2.5 → 0.625 — each step multiplies the error by (1 − 0.5), the steps shrink because the slope shrinks. That arithmetic is the widget, in one dimension.
